---
title: "Sarathy Engineering"
subtitle: "Architecture, patterns and the decisions behind a local-first personal AI assistant"
---


**Last updated:** 2026-10-04 · **Status:** living document · **Book version:** tracks release 0.15.0

Sarathy is a personal AI assistant built to run **locally**, on the operator's own
hardware, against local models. This book is the engineering record behind it: how
the system is put together, which patterns it leans on, and *why* each significant
decision was made the way it was.

It is written for engineers, not for users. If you want to install and run the
assistant, read the project README instead. If you want to know how the thing is
built and why it is built that way, you are in the right place.

## How to read this book {#sec-how-to-read}

The chapters are meant to be read in order, but they are independent:

| 2 | [Architecture](chapters/02-architecture.qmd) | How a message actually travels through the system |
| 3 | [Patterns](chapters/03-patterns.qmd) | The recurring design patterns, and the rules that keep them honest |

| — | [Engineering Log](engineering-log.qmd) | Dated, newest-first record of notable changes and lessons |

## House rules for this book {#sec-house-rules}

This book is destined for public hosting. Three rules are absolute, and they are
enforced mechanically by the smoke test rather than by good intentions:

1. **No personal information.** No real names — the book says "the operator", "the
   author", "the user". No chat identifiers, no contact details, no credentials of
   any kind.
2. **No private paths.** Everything is named relative to the repository root
   (`sarathy/agent/loop.py`) or relative to the *workspace* (`workspace/sessions/`).
   The machine's home directories are never spelled out.
3. **No private content.** Nothing from the operator's actual conversations, memory
   store or job records is quoted. The book describes *mechanisms*, never payloads.

Anything added to the book has to pass `python3 -m unittest discover tests -k book`,
which scans both the `.qmd` sources and the rendered `.html` for the patterns above.
See the update workflow in `doc/README.md` for how to add a chapter or a log entry.

## Provenance: how claims in this book are sourced {#sec-provenance}

Nothing here is invented. Every factual claim traces to one of four places, and the
book says which:

- **The code.** Repository-relative file paths and symbols, e.g.
  `sarathy/session/manager.py` (`SessionManager._should_rotate`).
- **The history.** Commits are referenced by their short hash and subject, e.g.
  `67a3176` *"rotate cron sessions at the trim cap"*.
- **The operator's engineering notes.** A small number of decisions are *not*
  visible in the code at all — they are operational practice (how work is
  delegated, how releases are tracked). Those are drawn from the author's notes
  and are labelled explicitly as such, because the repository cannot corroborate
  them.
- **Absence of evidence.** Where the repository contradicts an expectation, the book
  says so rather than papering over it. For example, there is no in-tree
  text-to-speech pipeline; see the media-handling pattern in Chapter 3.

A few figures appear repeatedly. Their sources, as of 2026-10-04:

| Figure | Value | Source |
|--------|-------|--------|
| Commits on `main` | 878 | `git log --oneline \| wc -l` |
| Declared package version | 0.15.0 | `pyproject.toml` |
| Python floor | 3.11 | `pyproject.toml` (`requires-python`) |
| Python lines in `sarathy/` | ~16.7k | `find sarathy -name '*.py' \| xargs wc -l` |
| Test modules | 36 | `ls tests/*.py` |
| Built-in channel adapters | 5 | `sarathy/channels/manager.py` |
| Built-in slash commands | 17 | `sarathy/agent/builtin_commands.py` |

## Where to start {#sec-where-to-start}

If you only read one diagram, read the [system map](chapters/02-architecture.qmd#fig-system-map)
in Chapter 2: one flowchart, one sequence diagram, and you understand the shape of
the whole thing.

If you only read one chapter, read Chapter 4. Every design decision that cost
something is written down there, including the ones that were wrong first.
